h1: 8 Vertical Mice That Actually Suit Laptop Setups, Ranked & Reviewed
metaTitle: Best Vertical Mice for Laptops: Ranked & Reviewed
metaDescription: Ranked and reviewed by Primea: 8 vertical mice for laptop users compared on USB-A ports, Bluetooth, size, battery and price, from under $25 to $100.
summary: The Logitech Lift is the best vertical mouse for a laptop because it has Bluetooth, so it needs no port, and a compact rechargeable body that slides into a bag. The ProtoArc EM11 NL is the cheaper compact choice if you have a spare USB-A port, the Lekvey adds a rechargeable battery for a desk-bound laptop, and the TECKNET and Anker wired models suit people who want zero pairing.
intro: Laptop owners make a specific mistake with vertical mice: they pick a mouse and forget the port. Thin laptops often have two USB-C ports and nothing else, so a mouse with a USB-A dongle means a little adapter you will lose within a month. Bluetooth sidesteps that, which is why connection type matters more here than it does for a desktop.

This ranking sorts eight vertical mice by how well they fit a laptop routine. We reviewed the listings and spec sheets for connection, battery, body size and price bucket, and we weighed portability heavily. A mouse that lives in a bag has to survive being jostled and charged rarely, so we favored compact shells and simple setup.

products.name: Logitech Lift Vertical Ergonomic Wireless Mouse
products.verdict: Bluetooth plus a dongle, a compact shell and a rechargeable battery make it the natural laptop partner.
products.description:
The Lift is a compact vertical mouse that offers both Bluetooth and a 2.4GHz dongle, with a rechargeable battery. That Bluetooth fallback is what makes it the strongest laptop pick, since the listing highlights it for mobile use.

It beats every other mouse here because it solves the port problem and the bag problem together. If your laptop has only USB-C, you simply pair over Bluetooth and leave the dongle behind. The shell is small enough for a sleeve pocket, and being rechargeable means no AA cells rattling around. The tradeoff is price: it is the most expensive mouse in this ranking, in the $50 to $100 range.

Buy it if your laptop travels with you and you want a vertical mouse that adapts to wherever you work. If you only use the laptop at one desk, a cheaper dongle model does the job.
pros: Bluetooth works on USB-C only laptops
Compact shell fits a laptop sleeve
Rechargeable battery means no spare cells
Dongle backup if Bluetooth misbehaves
cons: Gentler tilt than premium full-size rivals
products.idealFor: Travelling professionals and hybrid workers carrying a laptop daily.
products.skipIf: Your laptop sits on one desk and cost matters most.

products.name: ProtoArc EM11 NL Wireless Ergonomic Vertical Mouse, Rechargeable
products.verdict: A small rechargeable mouse with a USB-A dongle for travellers who watch their money.
products.description:
The EM11 NL has a compact rechargeable body and a 2.4GHz USB-A dongle. The listing calls out a solid review base, and the price falls in the budget-to-mid range.

It takes second because the small size and low weight suit a laptop bag, and the price is a fraction of the Lift. The compromise is the dongle: it needs a USB-A port, so a modern ultrabook needs an adapter, and there is no Bluetooth to fall back on.

Choose it if your laptop has a USB-A port and you want frequent-travel portability for little money. If your machine is USB-C only, spend a bit more on the Lift.
pros: Small body slips into any bag
Rechargeable cell avoids AA hassle
Very low price for the feature set
Solid owner feedback behind the listing
cons: USB-A dongle needs a port or adapter
products.idealFor: Budget travellers whose laptop still has a USB-A port.
products.skipIf: Your laptop has only USB-C ports.

products.name: Lekvey Ergonomic Mouse, Rechargeable Vertical Wireless Mouse
products.verdict: Mid-size, rechargeable and cheap, but it expects a USB-A port on your laptop.
products.description:
The Lekvey uses a 2.4GHz USB-A dongle and a built-in rechargeable battery in a mid-size body. It is listed in the under $25 range as a budget rechargeable.

It ranks third because its mid-size shell is less portable than the ProtoArc, though it gives average-sized hands a bit more room. Like the ProtoArc it has no Bluetooth, so USB-C-only laptops need an adapter.

It suits a laptop that lives docked at a desk, where portability matters less than hand comfort. Skip it if the laptop travels every day.
pros: Extra room for average-sized hands
Charges over USB, no battery buying
Budget price for a wireless model
Dongle needs no pairing steps
cons: Dongle ties up a USB-A port
products.idealFor: Docked laptop users with average-sized hands.
products.skipIf: You carry the mouse in a bag every day.

products.name: Anker 2.4G Wireless Ergonomic Mouse, Right Hand Vertical Mouse
products.verdict: A trusted-brand dongle mouse for people who don't mind swapping AA batteries.
products.description:
The Anker pairs a USB-A dongle with AA battery power in a moderate-size body. It is right-hand specific and sits in the under $25 bracket.

It lands fourth because AA cells and the right-handed shape limit it. On the plus side, a fresh AA can be bought in any shop if the mouse dies on a trip, which a rechargeable model cannot match mid-journey without a cable.

It works for budget buyers with a USB-A port who prefer to carry spare cells. If you want a left-handed or Bluetooth model, look elsewhere.
pros: Swap in a fresh AA anywhere
Known brand at a low price
Moderate tilt is easy to adopt
Plug-in dongle works instantly
products.idealFor: Right-handed laptop users who accept AA batteries.
products.skipIf: You want rechargeable or left-hand options.

products.name: Luhaso Ergonomic Vertical Wireless Mouse, 57 degree, Small/Medium Hands
products.verdict: A stated 57-degree angle in a body made for small to medium hands.
products.description:
The Luhaso advertises a 57-degree tilt and a body sized for small to medium hands, with a wireless connection and a budget price in the under $25 bucket.

It ranks fifth because the listing is thin on how the wireless link works and what powers it, so a laptop user cannot tell if it needs a USB-A port. Its sizing candor is a plus, since a small hand on a big mouse is a common complaint.

Consider it if you have smaller hands and want a stated angle cheaply. Check the product page for the connection type before you order for a USB-C laptop.
pros: Clear 57-degree angle on the listing
Sized honestly for smaller hands
Low price limits purchase risk
Compact enough for travel use
products.idealFor: Small-handed laptop users who want a defined tilt.
products.skipIf: You need to confirm Bluetooth support first.

products.name: Anker USB Wired Vertical Mouse, Ergonomic Mouse for Computer and Laptop
products.verdict: No battery, no dongle, no pairing; a cable and a plug.
products.description:
The Anker wired vertical mouse is marketed for computers and laptops alike. It connects over USB, has no battery, and is lighter for it, with a mid-range price in the $25 to $50 bucket.

It ranks sixth because a cable is awkward on a laptop that moves around, and the price is higher than the cheapest wireless options. Still, it removes every wireless failure mode: nothing to charge, nothing to pair, nothing to lose.

Choose it for a laptop that sits on a stand with an external monitor. A USB-C-only laptop will need an adapter for the plug.
pros: Nothing to charge, pair or lose
Light body without an internal battery
Explicitly marketed for laptop use
Works the moment it is plugged in
cons: Cable gets in the way when mobile
Costs more than cheaper wireless picks
products.idealFor: Laptops docked on a stand with an external display.
products.skipIf: You work from cafes or move rooms often.

products.name: TECKNET Wired Mouse, Comfortable Ergonomic Mouse with 6400 DPI
products.verdict: The cheapest wired option, with no dongle to lose and adjustable DPI.
products.description:
The TECKNET uses a wired USB-A connection and offers a 6400 DPI sensor with adjustable levels. The listing notes there is no dongle to lose, and the price is under $25.

It takes seventh place because it shares the wired limitations of the Anker but offers less brand backing. DPI adjustment is genuinely handy on a laptop, where a small trackpad-sized movement can need to cross a large external screen.

It works for a stationary laptop where you want the cheapest possible setup. Anyone moving between rooms should pick a wireless model.
pros: No dongle means nothing to lose
Adjustable DPI helps on big screens
Lowest price among the wired picks
Zero pairing or charging effort
cons: Cable is awkward for mobile use
Needs an adapter on USB-C laptops
products.idealFor: Stationary laptop users who want the lowest cost.
products.skipIf: You value portability or a premium finish.

products.name: Attoe Gaming Mouse with 5D Rocker, Wireless Vertical Mouse with 2400 DPI
products.verdict: A wireless mouse that stretches from spreadsheets into casual games.
products.description:
The Attoe is a wireless vertical mouse that adds a 2400 DPI sensor and a 5D rocker button, aimed at people who want office and light gaming duty from one device. The price is in the $25 to $50 bucket.

It finishes last because the listing has a small review sample and gives little on connection type, which is crucial for a laptop. The 5D rocker is a genuine extra, giving more inputs than the plain models.

Pick it if your laptop doubles as a casual gaming machine. For straight office use, the Lift or ProtoArc are safer.
pros: 5D rocker adds extra input options
Suits office work and casual play
Wireless link keeps the desk clean
Fair price for a hybrid design
products.idealFor: Laptop owners who game casually after work.
products.skipIf: You want a mouse with proven long-term reliability.

methodology.title: Port and connection fit
methodology.description: We checked whether each mouse needs USB-A, offers Bluetooth or plugs in by cable, because modern laptops often have only USB-C.

methodology.title: Portability
methodology.description: Body size, weight and battery type were judged for life in a bag, favoring compact rechargeable designs.

methodology.title: Ergonomic fit
methodology.description: Stated tilt angles and hand-size targets were compared, since a mouse that does not fit gets dropped within days.

methodology.title: Setup simplicity
methodology.description: Plug-in dongles and cables scored well for zero configuration, with Bluetooth credited when it saves a port.

methodology.title: Price and owner confidence
methodology.description: Each mouse was judged against its price bucket, and a thin review base lowered a score slightly.

whatMatters.detail: Many current laptops ship with only USB-C ports, while most budget vertical mice use a USB-A dongle. Without an adapter or Bluetooth, the mouse simply will not connect. Check your laptop's ports first, then read the listing for the words USB-A, Bluetooth or wired.

Bluetooth uses the laptop's built-in radio and keeps every port free, and it can pair with a phone or tablet. A dongle is stable and works instantly, but it takes a port and is easy to misplace. For a laptop that travels, Bluetooth is the safer bet.

A vertical mouse is taller than a normal one and takes more room in a laptop sleeve. Compact shells like the Lift and ProtoArc fit in a bag pocket, while full-size ones need real space. Compare dimensions on the listing before committing, and consider whether the mouse needs to leave your desk.

A rechargeable mouse needs a charge every so often, while an AA model needs spares. Wired mice need neither. Traveling users should favor rechargeable models and check whether the mouse can run while charging, which avoids stalling in the middle of a task.

People who move between a mouse and a laptop trackpad notice how DPI affects cursor travel across a big monitor. Adjustable DPI, as on the TECKNET, helps match the mouse to the screen. Check that the DPI button is easy to reach and that levels are listed.

howToChoose.intro: Your laptop's ports narrow the field faster than any other factor, so start there.

cards.label: Wired

cards.label: Wireless
cards.text: Cleaner desk and easier travel, with a dongle or Bluetooth. The Lift, ProtoArc and Lekvey cover most laptop users.

howToChoose.note: Go wireless unless your laptop stays docked all day.

cards.text: Bluetooth, a compact shell and a rechargeable battery, so one mouse moves between home and office without extra bits.

faq.q: Will a vertical mouse work with a USB-C only laptop?
faq.a: Only if it uses Bluetooth or you add a USB-A to USB-C adapter. Of the eight here, the Logitech Lift has Bluetooth, while the dongle and wired models need an adapter on a USB-C-only machine.

faq.q: What mistake do laptop owners make most?
faq.a: Buying a dongle mouse for a laptop with no spare USB-A port, then losing the adapter. Check your ports before ordering, or choose a Bluetooth mouse.

faq.q: Is a vertical mouse worth it over the trackpad?
faq.a: If you use a laptop for hours at a time, yes. An upright mouse supports a more natural forearm position than reaching for a trackpad, though you give up some portability. Keep a compact model in your bag for travel.

faq.q: How do I set up a Bluetooth mouse on a laptop?
faq.a: Switch the mouse to pairing mode, open the Bluetooth settings on your laptop and pick the mouse from the list. The Lift keeps its pairing for next time, and it can also use a dongle if Bluetooth misbehaves.

faq.q: Do I need to charge the mouse every day?
faq.a: No. Rechargeable models are designed to last much longer between charges than a laptop does. Top it up when convenient, and avoid letting it drain fully when you travel.

faq.q: Can I use a wired vertical mouse on a laptop?
faq.a: Yes, the Anker wired and TECKNET are both made for it. The cable can be awkward on a small desk, so they work best when the laptop is parked on a stand.

finalTake: The Logitech Lift is the vertical mouse to buy for a laptop, because Bluetooth keeps your ports free and the compact rechargeable body travels well. Choose the ProtoArc when you have a USB-A port and a tight budget, and go wired with the Anker if the laptop never leaves its stand. The rest are fine, but they ask you to compromise on ports, size or battery.
